set1.q: At which temperature does a thermally dimorphic fungus grow as unicellular yeast?
opts: 20 C lies in the natural-habitat range (below 30 C), where the fungus grows as a saprobic, multicellular mold that reproduces by sporulation. The unicellular yeast form needs the warmth of an animal host: 37 C.
25 C is room temperature, used for selective agar cultures that show the mold phase when the laboratory demonstrates dimorphism. The unicellular yeast form appears at 37 C, human body temperature.
30 C is the temperature at which dimorphic fungi grow as multicellular molds. They switch to unicellular yeasts at 37 C, human body temperature, inside the 35 to 40 C range of the animal habitat.

Correct. Thermally dimorphic fungi grow as multicellular molds at 30 C and as unicellular yeasts at 37 C, human body temperature; in the animal habitat (35 to 40 C) they live as parasitic, budding yeasts. Culturing at room temperature and at 37 C demonstrates the switch.

mis.20 C: natural-habitat temperature taken for host temperature
mis.30 C: mold temperature taken for yeast temperature

set1.q: How does Pneumocystis pneumonia become rapidly fatal when it is not controlled?
opts: Spherules with endospores form nodules

Spherules containing endospores and lung nodules come from inhaled Coccidioides arthrospores, and most such cases need no treatment at all. Pneumocystis pneumonia is deadly because its secretions block breathing.
Spread to the meninges and brain
Dissemination to the meninges and brain is how Cryptococcus neoformans causes severe neurological disturbance and death. Pneumocystis does its damage in the lungs, where secretions block breathing.
Secretions in the lungs block breathing
Correct. Pneumocystis pneumonia forms secretions in the lungs that block breathing; with cough, fever, shallow respiration and cyanosis, it can be rapidly fatal if not controlled with medication.
Fungal balls form in the lungs
Fungal balls form when Aspergillus spores germinate in the lungs, and invasive aspergillosis can add necrotic pneumonia. Pneumocystis kills by filling the lungs with secretions that block breathing.

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set1.q: What is the usual treatment for dermatophytoses?
opts: Removal of tissue and amphotericin B

Removal of affected tissues plus amphotericin B is the treatment for mucormycosis invading the nose, eyes, heart and brain. Dermatophytoses stay in the keratinized epidermis and respond to topical azoles over several weeks.
Immunization against the fungus

Immunization is typically ineffective against fungal infections because reinfection is exceedingly common. Dermatophytoses are treated, most often with topical azoles for several weeks, rather than prevented by a vaccine.
Topical azoles for several weeks

Correct. Treatment of dermatophytoses most often uses topical antifungal agents, azoles applied for several weeks, sometimes partnered with oral antifungal drugs if needed. Debridement of the skin and ultraviolet light treatments have also been successful.
Super-saturated potassium iodide

Super-saturated potassium iodide, with heat packs, treats sporotrichosis, a subcutaneous mycosis. Ringworm of the keratinized skin, hair and nails is treated mainly with topical azoles for several weeks.

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set1.q: Antibiotic therapy and catheters predispose patients to which opportunistic fungus?
opts: Cryptococcus species
Cryptococcus is associated with diabetes, tuberculosis, cancer, corticosteroids and immunosuppression. Antibiotic therapy and catheters are the predisposing conditions tied to Candida.
Fusarium species

Fusarium is a mainly tropical soil mold that infects eyes through contaminated contact lenses, toenails, feet and burned skin. Antibiotic therapy and catheters are the predisposing conditions tied to Candida.
Candida species

Correct. Among the common opportunistic fungi, Candida is the one associated with antibiotic therapy and catheters, alongside diabetes, corticosteroids and immunosuppression. It is the dominant opportunistic pathogen and its infections are usually endogenous.
Aspergillus species

Aspergillus is associated with leukemia, corticosteroids, tuberculosis, immunosuppression and intravenous drug abuse, not with antibiotic therapy or catheters. Those two predisposing conditions belong to Candida.

set1.q: From what source does the antifungal drug amphotericin B come?
opts: A soil mold of the genus Rhizopus

Rhizopus, with Mucor, is a Zygomycota mold that causes mucormycosis in people with diabetes, leukemia or malnutrition; amphotericin B is part of that infection's treatment, not a product of it. The drug comes from Streptomyces, a soil bacterium.
A soil bacterium of the genus Streptomyces

Correct. Amphotericin B is produced by a soil bacterium in the genus Streptomyces, yet it attacks fungal cells, which are eukaryotic. It is the highly toxic, often expensive drug of choice for many fungal infections.
A grain fungus of the genus Claviceps
Claviceps fungi contaminate rye and other grains as ergot, the source of mind-altering lysergic acid: a fungal toxin, not a drug. Amphotericin B comes from a soil bacterium, Streptomyces.
A soil mold of the genus Aspergillus
Aspergillus is a very common airborne soil fungus that causes aspergillosis, a disease amphotericin B is used to treat. The drug itself is made by a soil bacterium of the genus Streptomyces.

mis.A grain fungus of the genus Claviceps: fungal toxin source taken for drug source

set1.q: Which person best fits the risk profile for eumycetoma?
opts: A 45-year-old poorly fed harvester
A poorly nourished male harvester over 40 fits paracoccidioidomycosis of Central and South America. Eumycetoma's profile is younger: male, 11 to 30 years old, farming and not wearing shoes.
A kidney transplant recipient

Kidney transplant patients are at high risk for Pneumocystis pneumonia, an opportunist of the lungs. Eumycetoma is a deep tissue infection of young male farmers, 11 to 30 years old, who do not wear shoes.
A barefoot 20-year-old male farmer

Correct. Eumycetomas, deep tissue infections, are especially prevalent in poor countries, with risk factors of male sex, age 11 to 30 years, farming and not wearing shoes. Long-term antifungal drug therapy and amputation may be required for full resolution.
A 60-year-old road worker in dust

Increasing age and occupational exposure to dust or soil, as in road construction, are risk factors for Coccidioides immitis in the southwestern United States. Eumycetoma favors young male farmers, 11 to 30 years old, who go without shoes.

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set1.q: Which patients are at increased risk of invasive aspergillosis?
opts: Barefoot young male farmers

Male farmers aged 11 to 30 who do not wear shoes fit the risk profile for eumycetoma, a deep tissue infection of poor countries. Invasive aspergillosis threatens transplant recipients and cystic fibrosis patients.
Children lacking dietary protein

Children with too little protein intake (kwashiorkor) can develop a gastrointestinal form of mucormycosis. Invasive aspergillosis is a risk for organ and bone marrow transplant recipients and cystic fibrosis patients.
Obese patients with moist skin folds

Obese patients develop intertriginous Candida lesions in the armpits, groin and under the breasts, where skin stays moist. Invasive aspergillosis targets transplant recipients and cystic fibrosis patients.
Transplant and cystic fibrosis patients

Correct. Invasive aspergillosis can produce necrotic pneumonia and infection of the brain, heart and other organs, and transplant recipients (organ and bone marrow) are at increased risk, as are patients with cystic fibrosis.

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set1.q: Into what form do inhaled Blastomyces conidia convert in the lungs?
opts: Spherules full of endospores
Spherules filled with endospores are what Coccidioides forms in the lungs after its arthrospores are inhaled. Blastomyces conidia convert to yeasts instead, and the yeasts multiply there.
Branched septate hyphae
Hyphae are the mold form of the natural habitat below 30 C, and branched septate hyphae in sputum are typical of Aspergillus. At body temperature Blastomyces converts to multiplying yeasts.
Block-like arthroconidia

Block-like arthroconidia are the free-living form of Coccidioides, the form inhaled from dust; they are not a lung form of either fungus. Inhaled Blastomyces conidia become yeasts that multiply in the lungs.
Multiplying yeast cells

Correct. Blastomyces is a dimorphic fungus, free-living in soil; its inhaled conidia convert to yeasts that multiply in the lungs, the yeast phase that dimorphic fungi adopt at body temperature in an animal host.

set1.q: Which treatment is used for systemic sporotrichosis?
opts: Amphotericin B and/or itraconazole

Correct. Systemic sporotrichosis is treated with amphotericin B and/or itraconazole. Heat packs and/or super-saturated potassium iodide are the treatment given for infection of the appendages and lungs; once the disease is systemic, the drug pair is used.
Heat packs and/or potassium iodide

Heat packs and/or super-saturated potassium iodide are the treatment given for sporotrichosis of the appendages and lungs. For the systemic infection asked about here, the choice is amphotericin B and/or itraconazole.
Pentamidine and/or co-trimoxazole

Pentamidine, an antiprotozoal, and co-trimoxazole (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole), an antibacterial, treat Pneumocystis pneumonia and are not traditional antifungals. Systemic sporotrichosis is treated with the antifungals amphotericin B and/or itraconazole.
Topical azoles and debridement

Topical azoles for several weeks, sometimes with debridement or ultraviolet light, treat dermatophytoses that stay in keratinized skin. A systemic fungal infection needs systemic drugs: amphotericin B and/or itraconazole for sporotrichosis.

mis.Heat packs and/or potassium iodide: local treatment applied to systemic disease

set1.q: In which form of ringworm may nail extensions provide a portal of entry?
opts: Tinea unguium

Correct. Tinea unguium, ringworm of the nails, is a persistent colonization of the nails of the hands and feet that distorts the nail bed, and nail extensions may provide a portal of entry to the nail bed.
Tinea manuum
Tinea manuum is ringworm of the hand, found between the digits and spread by exposure to public surfaces. The nails, entered by way of nail extensions, belong to tinea unguium.
Tinea pedis
Tinea pedis is ringworm of the foot, between the digits and on the soles, picked up from public surfaces. The nail-bed form that nail extensions can open to the fungus is tinea unguium.
Tinea capitis
Tinea capitis involves the scalp and hair-bearing regions of the head, with possible hair loss, and is common in children. Persistent nail colonization that distorts the nail bed is tinea unguium.

mis.Tinea manuum: hand form confused with nail form
mis.Tinea pedis: foot form confused with nail form

set1.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire fungi of medical importance
set1.q: How do mycotoxicoses usually arise?
opts: Ingesting or inhaling fungal toxins

Correct. Mycotoxicoses are usually caused by ingesting or inhaling fungal toxins. Examples are aflatoxin on grains, corn and peanuts and ergot on rye or other grains contaminated by Claviceps fungi; they are intoxications, not infections.
Fungi invading through broken skin
Fungi entering through traumatized skin cause subcutaneous mycoses such as sporotrichosis, which are infections. Mycotoxicoses are intoxications by fungal toxins that are ingested or inhaled.
Spores provoking a hypersensitivity

Fungal spores provoking hypersensitivity, as in farmer's lung, cause atopic allergies, a separate category. Mycotoxicoses are poisonings by fungal toxins taken in by ingestion or inhalation, such as aflatoxin and ergot.
Overgrowth of resident yeast flora

Overgrowth of resident yeast is the usual, endogenous origin of Candida albicans infection. A mycotoxicosis is an intoxication: the person ingests or inhales a fungal toxin, as with aflatoxin or ergot.

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set1.q: A man from the midwestern United States has cough, chest pain and fever; a lung lesion on his chest X-ray is first taken for lung cancer, and his dog is sick with the same symptoms. Which fungus is the likely cause?
opts: Coccidioides immitis

Coccidioides is a southwestern United States fungus of alkaline, salty, semiarid soil that forms spherules in the lungs. A midwestern patient with a cancer-like lung lesion and a sick dog fits Blastomyces.
Paracoccidioides brasiliensis

Paracoccidioides is endemic in Central and South America and is usually a mild, self-limiting infection of rural farm workers. The midwestern setting, lung cancer mimic and sick dog point to Blastomyces.
Aspergillus fumigatus

Aspergillus fumigatus is an opportunist that threatens patients with human immunodeficiency virus infection, leukemia or transplants, forming fungal balls in the lungs. The midwestern setting, cancer-like lesion and sick dog fit Blastomyces.
Blastomyces dermatitidis

Correct. Blastomyces dermatitidis lives in the soil of the midwestern and southeastern United States; inhaled conidia multiply as yeasts in the lungs, the lesion may be mistaken for lung cancer on chest X-ray, and it causes cough, chest pain and fever in humans, dogs, cats and horses.

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set1.q: Which fungus causes the disease nicknamed 'Ohio Valley fever'?
opts: Histoplasma capsulatum

Correct. Histoplasmosis, 'Ohio Valley fever', is caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, the most common true fungal pathogen. It is known in the eastern and central United States and is now recognized as endemic in parts of Latin America and Africa.
Coccidioides immitis

Coccidioides immitis causes coccidioidomycosis, 'Valley fever' without the Ohio, mainly in the southwestern United States extending to Mexico and Central and South America. 'Ohio Valley fever' is histoplasmosis.
Blastomyces dermatitidis

Blastomyces dermatitidis causes North American blastomycosis, its own name, in the midwestern and southeastern United States and southern Canada. 'Ohio Valley fever' is the nickname of histoplasmosis.
Paracoccidioides brasiliensis
Paracoccidioides brasiliensis is endemic in Central and South America, the rarest of the primary mycoses, with no Ohio connection. 'Ohio Valley fever' is histoplasmosis, from Histoplasma capsulatum.

mis.Blastomyces dermatitidis: nickname given to a neighboring endemic fungus

set1.cite: PAJ5200.Fungi of Medical importance.pptx, Slide 26, 30, 33 and 37

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set1.q: What does Coccidioides form in the lungs after its spores are inhaled?
opts: Spherules that release endospores

Correct. An inhaled arthrospore develops into a spherule (a giant sporangium) that produces endospores, which are released in the lungs; the free-living stage, by contrast, is block-like arthroconidia. Immunocompetent people usually fight the infection off, while compromised people can develop meningitis, osteomyelitis and skin granulomas.
Yeasts that bud inside phagocytes
Yeasts that are phagocytosed and bud intracellularly are the tissue phase of Histoplasma, which is inhaled as microconidia. Coccidioides, after inhalation, forms spherules filled with endospores.
Fungal balls of septate hyphae
Fungal balls in the lungs and branched septate hyphae belong to Aspergillus, whose spores germinate in the lungs. Coccidioides, after inhalation, becomes spherules that release endospores.
Chains of block-like arthroconidia
Block-like arthroconidia are the free-living stage in soil, the form that is inhaled, not the lung form. Once in the lungs each arthrospore develops into a spherule that releases endospores.

mis.Chains of block-like arthroconidia: infective form taken for tissue form

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set1.q: A negative stain of a specimen shows encapsulated budding yeast. Which organism does this demonstrate?
opts: Pneumocystis jirovecii
Pneumocystis jirovecii is a small, unicellular fungus seen in tissue as cysts containing several bodies. Encapsulated budding yeast on negative stain is Cryptococcus neoformans.
Cryptococcus neoformans

Correct. A negative stain demonstrating encapsulated budding yeast is the picture of Cryptococcus neoformans, the widespread encapsulated yeast of pigeon-roost soil. Biochemical and serological testing are the best diagnostic tools for it.
Candida albicans
Candida albicans also buds, but its presumptive diagnosis rests on budding yeast cells with pseudohyphae, not a capsule. The capsule outlined by a negative stain marks Cryptococcus neoformans.
Aspergillus fumigatus
Aspergillus is seen as branched septate hyphae, for example in a sputum specimen, not as a budding yeast. An encapsulated budding yeast on negative stain is Cryptococcus neoformans.

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set1.q: On what basis do most scientists now classify Pneumocystis as a fungus rather than a protozoan?
opts: Its response to antifungals

Pneumocystis is treated with pentamidine (antiprotozoal) and co-trimoxazole (antibacterial), which are not traditional antifungal drugs, so drug response cannot be the basis. Genetic analysis is what places it among the fungi.
Its growth as hyphae
Pneumocystis is a small, unicellular fungus, seen in tissue as cysts containing several bodies, not as hyphae. Its fungal classification rests on genetic analysis.
Its antibody titers
Antibody titers show that human contact with Pneumocystis is very widespread and mostly asymptomatic; they do not show whether it is a fungus. The classification rests on genetic analysis.
Its genetic analysis

Correct. The taxonomy of Pneumocystis is still debated, fungus or protozoan, but most scientists lean toward a fungal classification because of genetic analysis. Its usual drugs do not settle the question: one is an antiprotozoal and the other an antibacterial.

mis.Its antibody titers: true fact answering a different question

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set1.q: A dye-stained sputum specimen shows a mass of branched septate hyphae and no yeast cells. Which fungus does this fit?
opts: Candida albicans

Candida albicans appears as budding or germinating yeast cells with young hyphae or pseudohyphae, typically from an oral or vaginal swab. A sputum mass of branched septate hyphae with no yeast cells fits Aspergillus.
Cryptococcus neoformans
Cryptococcus neoformans is an encapsulated budding yeast shown by a negative stain, not a mass of hyphae. Branched septate hyphae without any yeast cells point to Aspergillus, an airborne soil mold.
Coccidioides immitis
In the lungs Coccidioides forms spherules containing endospores, and in soil block-like arthroconidia; neither is a mass of branched septate hyphae in sputum. That pattern is Aspergillus.
Aspergillus species

Correct. Branched septate hyphae in a sputum specimen are the picture of Aspergillus, an airborne soil fungus whose spores germinate in the lungs and can form fungal balls. Dyes amplify these fungal elements in tissue specimens.

mis.Candida albicans: germinating yeast confused with septate hyphae
mis.Cryptococcus neoformans: encapsulated yeast confused with a mold

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set1.q: In which setting does cutaneous candidiasis typically occur?
opts: Skin punctured by thorns or wood

A thorn or wood puncture introduces Sporothrix schenckii, which forms a nodule and spreads to nearby lymph nodes. Cutaneous candidiasis needs no puncture; it develops in chronically moist skin and in burn patients.
Nail beds under nail extensions
Nail extensions may give a dermatophyte a portal to the nail bed in tinea unguium. Cutaneous candidiasis is a disease of chronically moist skin, such as skin folds in obese patients, and of burns.
Chronically moist skin and burns

Correct. Cutaneous candidiasis occurs in chronically moist areas of skin and in burn patients; intertriginous lesions in the armpits, groin and under the breasts are common in obese patients. The resident yeast takes hold where skin stays damp or damaged.
Gritty nodules on scalp hairs
Gritty, dark nodules on scalp hairs are black piedra, a superficial mycosis caused by Piedraia. Candida infects chronically moist skin, such as skin folds, and burned skin instead.

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set1.q: In the tissue phase of histoplasmosis, what happens to the fungus in the lungs?
opts: Its yeasts are killed once phagocytosed
Phagocytosis does not end the infection here: the yeasts multiply by budding inside the phagocytes, which in some cases enter the blood and cause disseminated disease in many organs.
Its yeasts are phagocytosed and bud inside

Correct. In the tissue phase the yeast form develops, is phagocytosed, and multiplies by budding intracellularly. Most patients recover without complications; in some, phagocytes enter the blood and carry the infection to many organs.
It forms spherules that release endospores

Spherules releasing endospores are the lung form of Coccidioides, which develop from inhaled arthrospores. Histoplasma's tissue phase is a yeast that is phagocytosed and then buds inside the phagocyte.
It stays a mold of branched hyphae
Branched septate hyphae in sputum are Aspergillus. Histoplasma is thermally dimorphic: at 37 C it grows as a yeast, which phagocytes engulf and inside which it multiplies by budding.

set1.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire fungi of medical importance
set1.q: Which factor may lead to white or black piedra?
opts: Poor hygiene, such as oily hair products

Correct. Both piedras are considered non-contagious and may result from poor personal hygiene, such as oily hair products and tight hats or veils. They are superficial mycoses of the hair shaft, and neither is common in the United States.
Close contact with an infected person

Both piedras are considered non-contagious, so close contact with an infected person is not how they arise. Person-to-person spread is a feature of the dermatophytes and Candida, which live on the human body.
Handling infected household animals

Animals are the main source of tinea barbae, a dermatophytosis of the chin and beard. The piedras are non-contagious and are linked to poor hygiene, such as oily hair products and tight hats or veils.
Inhaling spores from bird guano
Spores from soil rich in bird and bat guano are inhaled in histoplasmosis, a lung infection. The piedras sit on the hair shaft and are linked to poor hygiene: oily hair products, tight hats or veils.

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set1.q: On the World Health Organization's fungal priority list, which fungus is ranked one tier above Coccidioides?
opts: Histoplasma species

Correct. Coccidioides is in the medium priority group; Histoplasma species are in the high priority group, one tier above, with other Candida species, Fusarium, the eumycetoma agents and the Mucorales. The critical group sits above both.
Paracoccidioides species

Paracoccidioides species share the medium priority group with Coccidioides, Cryptococcus gattii and Pneumocystis jirovecii, so they sit level with it, not above. Histoplasma species are one tier up, in the high group.
Pneumocystis jirovecii

Pneumocystis jirovecii, the most prominent opportunistic infection in human immunodeficiency virus infection and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, is nonetheless medium priority, level with Coccidioides. Histoplasma is one tier above.
Cryptococcus gattii

Cryptococcus gattii is medium priority, level with Coccidioides, even though its relative Cryptococcus neoformans tops the critical group. Histoplasma species sit one tier above Coccidioides, in the high group.

mis.Pneumocystis jirovecii: clinical prominence taken for list rank
mis.Cryptococcus gattii: genus rank carried over to the species

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set1.q: Why do subcutaneous mycoses rarely spread throughout the body?
opts: Their capsules block entry into blood

A capsule is one of the fungal virulence factors and the mark of Cryptococcus neoformans, which does spread from the lungs to the meninges and brain. Subcutaneous fungi stay local for a different reason: the warmer blood and viscera inhibit them.
They cannot get past keratinized skin

Being confined to keratinized epidermis describes the dermatophytes of skin, hair and nails. Subcutaneous fungi go deeper, through traumatized skin into the tissue below, yet still rarely disseminate because the warmer blood and viscera inhibit them.
Cell-mediated immunity clears them early

Cell-mediated immunity is the host's most important antifungal defense, but subcutaneous mycoses are progressive and can destroy skin and underlying tissue, so they are not cleared early. Their spread is limited by the higher temperature of the blood and viscera.
Warmth of blood and viscera inhibits them

Correct. Most species that cause subcutaneous mycoses are greatly inhibited by the higher temperatures of the blood and viscera, so they rarely disseminate. They stay near the site where trauma introduced them, where the disease is progressive and can destroy skin and underlying tissue.
set1.cite: PAJ5200.Fungi of Medical importance.pptx, Slide 14, 15, 38, 42 and 56

set1.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire fungi of medical importance
set1.q: What is the main portal of entry for the primary (systemic) mycoses?
opts: Contamination of skin or hair surfaces
Surface contamination of skin or hair is the portal of the cutaneous and superficial mycoses, which stay in the outer layers. Primary (systemic) mycoses begin with spores inhaled from the air.
Shared exercise equipment

Fomites such as shared exercise equipment spread dermatophytes and Candida, which live on the body. The primary mycoses are generally not communicable; their portal is the respiratory tract, by inhaled spores.
Spores inhaled from the air

Correct. The primary mycoses enter by the respiratory portal: spores in the air are inhaled when soil or animal waste containing conidia is disturbed, and they germinate in the lungs into yeast or yeast-like cells. From there infection can become systemic in some hosts.
Trauma that inoculates skin or nails

Trauma that inoculates skin or nails is the portal of the subcutaneous mycoses. Spores of true pathogens can occasionally enter broken skin, but the main portal of the primary mycoses is the respiratory tract.
set1.cite: PAJ5200.Fungi of Medical importance.pptx, Slide 12, 14 and 24

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set1.q: Which description fits paracoccidioidomycosis?
opts: An opportunist needing impaired defenses
Paracoccidioides is a primary (true) fungal pathogen of rural farm workers, not an opportunist defined by impaired defenses. It causes the rarest primary mycosis, usually mild and self-limiting.
Rarest primary mycosis, usually mild

Correct. Paracoccidioidomycosis, endemic in Central and South America (mainly the cool, humid soils of Brazil, Colombia, Venezuela, Argentina and Paraguay), is the rarest of the primary mycoses; systemic disease is not common, and infections are usually mild and self-limiting.
Commonest primary mycosis, usually mild

Mildness is right, but rarity is reversed: the most common true fungal pathogen is Histoplasma capsulatum, cause of 'Ohio Valley fever', while Paracoccidioides causes the rarest of the primary mycoses.
Rarest primary mycosis, usually systemic
Rarity is right, but severity is overstated: systemic paracoccidioidomycosis is not common. Lung or skin infections, from inhaled or inoculated spores, are usually mild and self-limiting.

set1.q: A fungus with few, if any, virulence factors causes a systemic infection in a patient taking long-term corticosteroids. How is this mycosis best classified?
opts: Dermatophytosis

Dermatophytoses are strictly confined to keratinized epidermis (skin, hair, scalp and nails), so they are not systemic. A low-virulence fungus causing systemic disease in a patient on corticosteroids is an opportunistic mycosis.
Opportunistic mycosis

Correct. Few, if any, virulence factors plus a host weakened by corticosteroids is the picture of an opportunistic mycosis: these fungi usually start infection in immunocompromised hosts, and predisposing factors such as primary illness, corticosteroid use, diabetes and cancer should be considered.
True (primary) mycosis

A true pathogen can invade and grow in a healthy host and does not depend on a weakened one. A fungus with few, if any, virulence factors striking a patient on corticosteroids is an opportunist; the tell is the impaired host.
Subcutaneous mycosis

Subcutaneous mycoses begin when trauma inoculates the fungus into the skin or nails, a level of invasion rather than a degree of pathogenicity. This infection is systemic and arose in a corticosteroid-weakened host from a low-virulence fungus, which marks it as opportunistic.

set1.q: Which conditions promote dermatophyte infection?
opts: Abraded skin and close contact

Correct. Hardy dermatophyte spores, abraded skin and close person-to-person or person-to-fomite contact promote infection. The natural reservoirs are humans, animals and soil, and shared items such as exercise equipment can carry the fungus from one person to the next.
Corticosteroids and diabetes

Corticosteroids, diabetes and other impaired defenses predispose to the opportunistic mycoses, such as candidiasis and cryptococcosis. Dermatophytes need no such weakness: their hardy spores infect abraded skin through close contact with people or fomites.
Inhaling dust from disturbed soil

Dust from disturbed soil carries the conidia of the true fungal pathogens into the lungs. Dermatophytes are not inhaled; their hardy spores infect abraded skin through close contact with people or fomites.
Puncture wounds from plant thorns

A thorn puncture carries subcutaneous fungi such as Sporothrix schenckii into deeper tissue. Dermatophytes stay in keratinized epidermis and spread by close contact with people or fomites onto abraded skin.

set1.q: In the laboratory workup of hair, skin and nail specimens for fungi, which method is applied directly to the hairs?
opts: Inoculation of animals

Animal inoculation is reserved for diagnosing systemic mycoses when other methods are unavailable or indeterminate, not for hair, skin or nail specimens. Hairs are examined directly under Wood's light.
Examination under Wood's light

Correct. For hair, skin and nail specimens the identification pathway uses Wood's light on the hairs, alongside a hot potassium hydroxide wet mount, brighteners and periodic acid-Schiff staining, before culture on selective media for 4 weeks and a hair infection test.
Negative stain for a capsule
A negative stain for a capsule is used on sputum to show encapsulated yeasts such as Cryptococcus; it is not the direct examination of hairs. Hairs are examined under Wood's light.
Germ tube test in serum

The germ tube test identifies yeasts that sprout hyphal tubes after 2 to 4 hours in serum, among the tests for blood, cerebrospinal fluid, pus and vaginal secretion isolates. Hairs are examined directly under Wood's light.

set1.q: How does amphotericin B damage fungal cells?
opts: It blocks the mold-to-yeast switch

Thermal dimorphism, the switch from hyphae to yeasts at 37 C, is a fungal virulence factor, but amphotericin B does not act on it. The drug complexes with membrane lipids so that cytoplasmic ions seep out.
It strips away the fungal capsule
Capsules are a virulence factor of some fungi, shown by a negative stain, not the drug's target. Amphotericin B complexes with membrane lipids, opening the membrane so that cytoplasmic ions leak out.
It binds membrane lipids, opening leaks

Correct. Amphotericin B forms complexes with fungal cell membrane lipids, causing openings through which cytoplasmic ions seep out. The action is not selective enough to spare human cells, since fungi and humans are both eukaryotes, hence its toxicity.
It dissolves the thick fungal cell wall

The thick cell wall is what lets fungi survive potassium hydroxide, which lyses human cells instead; it is not the drug's target. Amphotericin B acts on the cell membrane, complexing with its lipids so ions leak out.

set1.q: Where is Cryptococcus neoformans found in the environment?
opts: Rye and other cereal grains
Rye and other grains contaminated by Claviceps fungi carry ergot, a cause of mycotoxicosis. Cryptococcus neoformans is an encapsulated yeast of the soil around urban pigeon roosts and decaying wood.
Soil near urban pigeon roosts

Correct. Cryptococcus neoformans is a widespread encapsulated yeast that inhabits soil around pigeon roosts in urban areas, as well as soil containing decaying wood. Healthy humans are strongly resistant, so frank infection occurs in immunocompromised patients.
Alkaline, salty semiarid soil

Alkaline, salty soils in semiarid, hot climates hold Coccidioides immitis, spread by drought, rain and windstorms. Cryptococcus neoformans lives instead in soil around urban pigeon roosts and in soil containing decaying wood.
Normal flora of mouth and skin

Living as normal flora of the mouth and skin describes Candida albicans, whose infections are usually endogenous. Cryptococcus neoformans comes from the environment: soil around urban pigeon roosts and soil with decaying wood.

set1.q: Which ability defines a true (primary) fungal pathogen?
opts: Staying a mold at human body temperature

This reverses thermal dimorphism: these fungi grow as molds at 30 C but switch to yeasts at 37 C, human body temperature. The switch is their adaptation to the host; the defining ability is invading and growing in a healthy host.
Invading and growing in a healthy host

Correct. A true or primary fungal pathogen can invade and grow in a healthy host. Its most striking adaptation is the switch from hyphal cells to yeast cells with the change to host temperature. An opportunist, by contrast, has little or no virulence of its own and needs impaired host defenses.
Needing impaired host defenses to infect

Needing impaired defenses (human immunodeficiency virus infection, cancer, diabetes) describes an opportunistic fungal pathogen, which has little or no virulence of its own. A true pathogen needs no such help: it invades and grows in a healthy host.
Spreading readily from person to person

Most fungal pathogens do not need a host to complete their life cycles, so their infections are generally not communicable; the person-to-person spreaders are the dermatophytes and Candida, which live on the body. A true pathogen is defined by invading a healthy host.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set2.q: A woman has had several episodes of vaginal yeast infection over the years. Which statement about immunity to opportunistic fungi like this one is accurate?
opts: Healthy people have no defense to them

Humans are relatively resistant to fungi while the immune system is competent: skin, mucous membranes, cilia, cell-mediated immunity, phagocytosis and inflammation all defend. What is missing against opportunists is lasting immunity, so reinfection is likely.
Reinfection with them is highly likely

Correct. Lasting immunity develops against some true fungal pathogens rather than opportunists, so reinfection with opportunistic fungi is highly likely; repeated episodes of vaginal yeast infection or foot fungus are the familiar result. The same fact is why immunization against fungi is typically ineffective.
One episode leaves lasting immunity

Long-term immunity does not follow infection with opportunistic fungi; reinfection is highly likely, which is why her episodes keep recurring. The recurrence itself is the tell that no protective immunity formed.
Vaccination prevents further episodes
Immunization is typically ineffective against fungal infections precisely because reinfection is exceedingly common. Control relies on antifungal drugs such as azoles and nystatin, not on vaccines.

set2.q: A man with diabetes has the thick, white, adherent growth on the tongue shown. Which finding in a scraping would support a presumptive diagnosis?
opts: Encapsulated yeast on negative stain

An encapsulated budding yeast on negative stain identifies Cryptococcus neoformans, which infects the lungs and meninges. Thrush on the tongue is Candida albicans, presumptively diagnosed by budding yeast cells with pseudohyphae.
Branched septate hyphae in sputum

Branched septate hyphae, as seen in a sputum specimen, point to Aspergillus, whose spores form fungal balls in the lungs. A white oral growth calls for Candida's own finding: budding yeast cells and pseudohyphae.
Cysts containing several bodies

Cysts containing several bodies are the tissue form of Pneumocystis jirovecii, a cause of pneumonia in immunocompromised hosts. Thrush is a Candida albicans infection, supported by budding yeast cells and pseudohyphae.
Budding yeast cells and pseudohyphae

Correct. A thick, white, adherent growth on the mucous membranes of the mouth in a man with diabetes is thrush, from Candida albicans. A presumptive diagnosis is made when budding yeast cells and pseudohyphae are found; growth on selective, differential media then tells the Candida species apart.

set2.q: Why are most fungal infections generally not communicable from one person to another?
opts: People rarely meet fungal spores

Molds and yeasts are widely distributed in air, dust, fomites and normal flora, so exposure is common. Spread from person to person is uncommon because most fungi complete their life cycles without a host.
The fungi need no host for their life cycle

Correct. Most fungal pathogens do not require a host to complete their life cycles: they live free in soil or other matter and infect when it is disturbed, so their infections are generally not communicable. The exceptions, dermatophytes and Candida, live on the body and do pass person to person.
The fungi die at human body temperature

Body temperature does not kill true pathogens: at 37 C they switch from molds to yeasts and keep growing in the host. Their infections are not communicable because the fungi need no host to complete their life cycles.
One infection leaves lasting immunity

Reinfection is highly likely with opportunistic fungi, so immunity cannot be what stops spread between people. Most fungal infections are not communicable because the fungi need no host to complete their life cycles.

set2.q: How is tinea pedis mainly spread?
opts: Exposure to public surfaces

Correct. Tinea pedis (foot) and tinea manuum (hand) are spread by exposure to public surfaces and occur between the digits and on the soles. Tellingly, tinea pedis is rare where people usually go barefoot, so it is the shared surfaces, not bare feet, that matter.
Contact with infected animals
Contact with animals is the main source of tinea barbae, ringworm of the chin and beard of adult males. The foot form, tinea pedis, comes from exposure to public surfaces.
Puncture by thorns or splinters

A thorn or splinter puncture introduces subcutaneous fungi such as Sporothrix schenckii into deeper tissue. Tinea pedis is a cutaneous infection of the keratinized skin of the foot, picked up from public surfaces.
Going barefoot as a daily habit
Tinea pedis is rare where people usually go barefoot, so daily bare feet are not its source. It spreads by exposure to public surfaces and settles between the digits and on the soles.

set2.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire fungi of medical importance
set2.q: Which weather pattern most enhances the spread of Coccidioides?
opts: Cold, wet weather after a warm, dry spell

Sporulation in colder, wetter weather after a warm, dry dormancy is the pattern of Blastomyces dermatitidis in the midwestern and southeastern United States. Coccidioides spreads with drought, heavy rain and then windstorms.
Steady rain through winter and spring

Coccidioides remains dormant in winter and spring, so steady seasonal rain is not its spreading pattern. Its spread is driven by cycles of drought and heavy rain followed by windstorms that lift spore-laden dust.
Cool, humid conditions year-round

Cool, humid soils are the setting of Paracoccidioides in Central and South America. Coccidioides belongs to hot, semiarid climates with alkaline, salty soil, spread by drought, heavy rain and windstorms.
Drought, then heavy rain, then windstorms

Correct. Coccidioides lives in alkaline, salty soils of semiarid, hot climates, and its spread is greatly enhanced by cycles of drought and heavy rains followed by windstorms that raise spore-laden dust. It remains dormant in winter and spring.

mis.Steady rain through winter and spring: dormant season taken for active season

set2.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire fungi of medical importance
set2.q: Where does Histoplasma capsulatum grow in nature?
opts: Cool, humid soils of South America

Cool, humid soils of Brazil, Colombia, Venezuela, Argentina and Paraguay are where Paracoccidioides brasiliensis lives. Histoplasma grows in moist soil rich in nitrogen, especially with bird and bat guano.
Decaying plants, pine straw and hay

Decaying plant matter, pine straw and hay bales are the haunts of Sporothrix schenckii, a saprobe that enters through puncture wounds. Histoplasma's home is moist, nitrogen-rich soil with bird and bat guano.
Moist, nitrogen-rich soil with guano

Correct. Histoplasma capsulatum grows in moist soil with a high nitrogen content, especially soil containing bird and bat guano. When wind or digging disturbs that soil, the conidia become airborne and are inhaled.
Alkaline, salty soil of hot, dry land

Alkaline, salty soil in semiarid, hot climates is the home of Coccidioides immitis, whose spread is boosted by drought, heavy rain and windstorms. Histoplasma needs moist, nitrogen-rich soil, especially with guano.

set2.q: Which pair of predisposing conditions is associated with Aspergillus?
opts: Antibiotic therapy and catheters

Antibiotic therapy and catheters are the predisposing conditions tied to Candida, along with diabetes, corticosteroids and immunosuppression. Aspergillus is linked to leukemia, tuberculosis and intravenous drug abuse.
Third-degree burns and intravenous therapy
Third-degree burns and intravenous therapy predispose to the Zygomycota species, together with diabetes, cancer and corticosteroids. Aspergillus is linked to leukemia and intravenous drug abuse.
Kwashiorkor and malnutrition

Malnutrition, including the protein deficiency kwashiorkor in children, sets the stage for mucormycosis. Aspergillus is associated with leukemia, corticosteroids, tuberculosis, immunosuppression and intravenous drug abuse.
Leukemia and intravenous drug abuse

Correct. Aspergillus is associated with leukemia, corticosteroids, tuberculosis, immunosuppression and intravenous drug abuse. Leukemia also appears among the patients for whom Aspergillus is a serious opportunistic threat, with human immunodeficiency virus infection and transplants.

set2.q: Along with amphotericin B, what does treatment of mucormycosis involve?
opts: Removal of affected tissues

Correct. Treatment of mucormycosis involves removal of affected tissues plus amphotericin B. Surgical removal of damaged tissue is necessary in some fungal infections, and mucormycosis, which invades the nose, eyes, heart and brain with severe consequences, is one of them.
Heat packs over the lesions

Heat packs, with or without super-saturated potassium iodide, are used for sporotrichosis of the appendages and lungs. Invasive mucormycosis is treated by removing affected tissues and giving amphotericin B.
Ultraviolet light treatments
Ultraviolet light treatments, like debridement, have helped in dermatophytoses of the keratinized skin. Mucormycosis invades deep membranes and needs removal of affected tissue with amphotericin B.
Immunizing close contacts

Immunization is typically ineffective against fungal infections because reinfection is exceedingly common, and most fungal infections are not communicable to other persons. Treatment combines tissue removal with amphotericin B.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set2.q: Which tissues do dermatophytes infect?
opts: Subcutaneous tissue after trauma
Subcutaneous tissue is reached when a puncture wound carries fungi such as Sporothrix schenckii through traumatized skin. Dermatophytes stay in the keratinized layer: skin, hair, scalp and nails.
Mucous membranes of mouth and throat

A thick, white, adherent growth on the mucous membranes of the mouth and throat is thrush, caused by Candida albicans. Dermatophytes are confined to keratinized epidermis: skin, hair, scalp and nails.
The lungs after inhaled spores

The lungs, reached by inhaled spores through the respiratory portal, are where the primary mycoses such as histoplasmosis begin. Dermatophytes infect keratinized epidermis after contamination of the skin or hair surface.
Keratinized skin, hair and nails

Correct. Dermatophytoses (ringworm or tinea) are infections strictly confined to the keratinized epidermis: skin, hair, scalp and nails. They begin with contamination of the skin or hair surface rather than with inhaled spores or a deep puncture.

set2.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire fungi of medical importance
set2.q: Blastomyces dermatitidis lives in forest soil, decaying wood and animal manure. How do people usually acquire it?
opts: From an infected person's cough
Most fungal pathogens do not need a host to complete their life cycles, so their infections are generally not communicable. Blastomyces is acquired from its soil habitat by inhaling conidia.
Through sexual contact
Sexual contact is one way Candida albicans spreads, a yeast of the human body, not a soil fungus like Blastomyces dermatitidis. Its conidia are inhaled from soil, decaying wood or manure.
By eating crops grown in it
Ingestion is the route of fungal toxins (mycotoxicoses such as aflatoxin from grains, corn and peanuts), not of Blastomyces. Its conidia are inhaled and convert to yeasts in the lungs.
By inhaling its conidia

Correct. People inhale the conidia from the disturbed soil; as few as 10 to 100 inhaled conidia convert to yeasts and multiply in the lungs, causing cough, chest pain and fever. Chronic skin nodules and later bone and nervous system complications can follow.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set2.q: Why is immunization typically ineffective for preventing fungal infections?
opts: Fungi cause too few human infections

Fungi are relatively nonpathogenic, yet they still cause the dermatophytoses (the most prevalent fungal diseases), fatal systemic disease and a rising share of nosocomial infections. The stated reason vaccines fail is that reinfection is exceedingly common.
Fungi turn into yeasts inside the host

Thermal dimorphism, the switch to yeasts at body temperature, is a survival adaptation of true pathogens, not the reason given for vaccine failure. Immunization is ineffective because reinfection is exceedingly common.
Antifungal drugs already prevent infection

Antifungal drugs such as amphotericin B, flucytosine, azoles and nystatin treat infection; they are not the means of prevention. Prevention is limited to respirator masks and protective clothing, and vaccines fail because reinfection is so common.
Reinfection is exceedingly common

Correct. Immunization is typically ineffective against fungal infections because reinfection is exceedingly common. Control therefore relies on antifungal drugs (amphotericin B, flucytosine, azoles and nystatin), surgical removal of damaged tissue where needed, and limiting contact with spores.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set2.q: Yeast cells of a dimorphic fungus leave the animal host and return to the soil. What happens to them?
opts: They form spherules filled with endospores

Spherules with endospores are the form Coccidioides takes in the lungs, inside the host; its free-living stage is block-like arthroconidia. Yeasts that leave a host revert to the sporulating hyphal state.
They die at the lower temperature

Below 30 C is the natural habitat of the free-living mold, not a lethal condition. The yeasts revert to the sporulating hyphal state, a conversion that can even be demonstrated on artificial media in the laboratory.
They revert to the sporulating hyphal form

Correct. Yeast cells leaving the animal host return to the environment and revert to the sporulating hyphal state, helped by decreased temperature, optimal oxygen and improved nutrients. Outside a host the fungus lives as a saprobic, free-living mold below 30 C; the conversion can be shown on laboratory media.
They stay yeasts and bud in the soil

Budding is how the yeast phase reproduces inside the animal host, at 35 to 40 C. In the natural habitat, below 30 C, the fungus is a saprobic mold that reproduces by sporulation, so the yeasts revert to hyphae.

set2.q: When is animal inoculation used in identifying a fungal pathogen?
opts: As the first step for every sputum sample

Sputum is first digested to remove debris, then examined by negative stain, potassium hydroxide mount and special stains, and cultured for up to 8 weeks. Animals are inoculated only for systemic mycoses when other methods fail.
To demonstrate thermal dimorphism in culture

Dimorphism is shown by culturing on selective agar at room temperature (25 or 30 C) and on blood agar at 37 C. Animal inoculation is for systemic mycoses when other methods are unavailable or indeterminate.
To diagnose superficial hair and nail infections

Hair, skin and nail specimens are worked up with Wood's light, potassium hydroxide, brighteners, stains, culture and a hair infection test; no animals are used. Animal inoculation is for systemic mycoses when other methods fail.
For systemic mycoses when other methods fail

Correct. Animal inoculation is performed only to help diagnose systemic mycoses when other methods are unavailable or indeterminate. Stains, culture on selective and differential media, and biochemical, antigen and serological tests come first.

set2.q: Why does Sabouraud dextrose agar favor the growth of fungi over bacteria?
opts: Its dyes stain the fungal cell walls

Dyes and brighteners are applied to specimens to make fungal elements stand out under the microscope; they are not what makes the agar selective. The agar favors fungi through its fairly low pH and added antibacterial chemicals.
Its fairly low pH inhibits most bacteria

Correct. Sabouraud dextrose agar has a fairly low pH, which inhibits most bacteria but not fungi, and specific chemicals may be added to block bacterial growth further. That makes it the commonly used selective medium for culturing fungi.
Its high pH inhibits most bacteria
The pH runs the other way: Sabouraud dextrose agar is fairly acidic, and that low pH is what inhibits most bacteria while fungi keep growing. A high pH is not its selective feature.
Its low pH inhibits fungi, not bacteria

This turns the selectivity around: the low pH of Sabouraud dextrose agar inhibits most bacteria but not fungi. A medium that held fungi back would be useless for culturing them; fungi tolerate the acidity.

set2.q: Which fungus does the World Health Organization rank as its number one critical fungal pathogen?
opts: Candida auris

Candida auris is critical and emerging, a cause of hospital outbreaks that are difficult to eradicate, but it is not ranked first. Cryptococcus neoformans holds the number one place on the critical list.
Histoplasma capsulatum

Histoplasma capsulatum is the most common true fungal pathogen, but on the World Health Organization's list Histoplasma species are high priority, not critical. Number one critical is Cryptococcus neoformans.
Cryptococcus neoformans

Correct. Cryptococcus neoformans, an encapsulated yeast of soil around urban pigeon roosts and of soil with decaying wood, is the number one critical fungal pathogen on the World Health Organization's list. The other critical members are Aspergillus fumigatus, Candida albicans and Candida auris.
Aspergillus fumigatus

Aspergillus fumigatus is critical, but it is number three on the list; it is the most common Aspergillus species in human disease. Number one is Cryptococcus neoformans, the encapsulated yeast of pigeon-roost soil.

set2.q: Which organism causes tinea versicolor?
opts: Trichophyton, a dermatophyte
Trichophyton is a dermatophyte genus that causes ringworm of keratinized skin, hair and nails. Despite its tinea name, tinea versicolor is a superficial mycosis caused by the yeast Malassezia furfur.
Piedraia, a piedra agent
Piedraia causes black piedra, dark-brown to black gritty nodules on scalp hairs. The mild scaling and mottling of the skin in tinea versicolor come from the yeast Malassezia furfur.
Candida albicans, a yeast

Candida albicans is also a yeast, but on the skin it causes cutaneous candidiasis in chronically moist areas and in burn patients. The chronic scaling and mottling of tinea versicolor are caused by Malassezia furfur.
Malassezia furfur, a yeast

Correct. Tinea versicolor is caused by a yeast, Malassezia furfur, and elicits mild, chronic scaling and mottling of the skin. The same yeast is also implicated in folliculitis, psoriasis and seborrheic dermatitis.

set2.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire fungi of medical importance
set2.q: Besides arising from a person's own flora, how can Candida albicans be spread?
opts: Thorn and wood splinter punctures
A thorn or wood puncture plants Sporothrix schenckii, a soil saprobe, under the skin. Candida albicans passes between people through surgery, childbirth, breast-feeding and sexual contact.
Eating moldy grain or peanuts

Eating grains, corn or peanuts carrying aflatoxin causes a mycotoxicosis, a poisoning by a fungal toxin. Candida albicans infection spreads from person to person through surgery, childbirth, breast-feeding and sexual contact.
Childbirth, breast-feeding and sex

Correct. Candida albicans is a widespread yeast that is usually endogenous and not always considered contagious, yet it can be spread through surgery, childbirth, breast-feeding and sexual contact. Vulvovaginal infection may pass to unprotected sexual partners, especially uncircumcised males.
Soil around urban pigeon roosts

Soil around urban pigeon roosts and soil with decaying wood are the home of Cryptococcus neoformans, an environmental yeast. Candida albicans lives on people and is spread through surgery, childbirth, breast-feeding and sexual contact.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set2.q: Farmer's lung, teapicker's lung and bark stripper's disease are examples of which kind of fungal illness?
opts: Hypersensitivity to fungal spores

Correct. Fungal spores are common sources of atopic allergies or hypersensitivities, and farmer's lung, teapicker's lung and bark stripper's disease are grouped with seasonal allergies and asthma rather than with infections or the toxin-caused mycotoxicoses.
Mycotoxicosis from eaten toxins

Mycotoxicoses come from ingesting or inhaling fungal toxins, such as aflatoxin in grains, corn and peanuts or ergot on rye. Farmer's lung and its relatives are atopic allergies (hypersensitivities) to fungal spores.
Invasive opportunistic mycosis

Invasive opportunistic mycoses, such as aspergillosis or mucormycosis, need impaired host defenses and tissue invasion. Farmer's lung, teapicker's lung and bark stripper's disease are hypersensitivities to fungal spores.
Subcutaneous mycosis from trauma

Subcutaneous mycoses follow trauma that carries fungi into the skin, as with sporotrichosis from thorns. These occupational lung conditions are hypersensitivity reactions to fungal spores, grouped with seasonal allergies and asthma.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set2.q: Beyond intact skin, mucous membranes and respiratory cilia, which host defense is among the most important against fungi?
opts: Immunity left by a past infection

With opportunistic fungi reinfection is highly likely (think of repeated vaginal yeast infections or foot fungus), so a past infection is not a dependable shield. The defenses named as most important are cell-mediated immunity, phagocytosis and inflammation.
An acidic, low-pH environment

A low pH inhibits most bacteria but not fungi; that is exactly why Sabouraud dextrose agar is acidic, to grow fungi while holding bacteria back. Acidity is no antifungal defense; cell-mediated immunity, phagocytosis and inflammation are the most important.
Cell-mediated immunity

Correct. Skin, mucous membranes and cilia are the barriers; the most important defenses are cell-mediated immunity (T cells and their cytokines), phagocytosis and inflammation. That is why impaired immunity, as in human immunodeficiency virus infection or cancer, opens the door to opportunistic fungi.
Vaccine-induced antibody

Immunization is typically ineffective against fungal infections because reinfection is exceedingly common, so vaccine antibody is not a defense to rely on. The most important defenses are cell-mediated immunity, phagocytosis and inflammation.

mis.An acidic, low-pH environment: antibacterial condition assumed to work on fungi

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set2.q: Which regimen does systemic cryptococcal infection generally require?
opts: Heat packs plus potassium iodide

Heat packs and/or super-saturated potassium iodide treat sporotrichosis of the appendages and lungs, a subcutaneous mycosis. Systemic cryptococcosis, which can reach the brain, needs amphotericin B and an azole such as fluconazole.
Topical azoles for weeks

Topical azoles applied for several weeks are the usual treatment for dermatophytoses of keratinized skin, hair and nails. A systemic infection such as cryptococcosis needs amphotericin B with fluconazole or another azole.
Amphotericin B plus an azole

Correct. Systemic cryptococcal infection generally requires amphotericin B and fluconazole or another azole-type drug. Treatment protocols are well established for patients with human immunodeficiency virus infection, though the drugs may be unavailable in many countries.
Pentamidine plus co-trimoxazole

Pentamidine, an antiprotozoal, and co-trimoxazole, an antibacterial, treat Pneumocystis pneumonia and are not traditional antifungals. Cryptococcosis is treated with the antifungals amphotericin B and fluconazole or another azole.

set2.q: Contaminated plant material pierces a gardener's skin, and Sporothrix schenckii forms a nodule at the site. Where does the infection typically spread next?
opts: To nearby lymph nodes

Correct. In the lymphocutaneous variety, contaminated plant material penetrates the skin, the fungus forms a nodule at the site, and the infection then spreads to nearby lymph nodes. It rarely disseminates further, because the warmer blood and viscera inhibit subcutaneous fungi.
To the meninges and brain

Spread from the lungs to the meninges and brain, with severe neurological disturbance and death, is the path of Cryptococcus neoformans in compromised hosts. Sporothrix schenckii in the skin moves from its nodule to nearby lymph nodes and seldom goes deeper.
Into the blood and viscera

Subcutaneous fungi are greatly inhibited by the higher temperatures of the blood and viscera, so they rarely disseminate that way. The usual path from a Sporothrix nodule is to the nearby lymph nodes.
Into the sinuses and ear canals
Colonizing the sinuses, ear canals, eyelids and conjunctiva is a feature of Aspergillus, an airborne soil fungus. A Sporothrix nodule from a skin puncture spreads instead to the nearby lymph nodes.

set2.q: A 58-year-old African-American man who repairs roads in the southwestern United States develops a lung infection after a dust storm. Which fungus is the most likely cause?
opts: Coccidioides immitis

Correct. The southwestern United States, road repair and a dust storm are classic exposures for Coccidioides immitis (Valley fever), and African or African-American descent, increasing age (over 40 to 60 years) and occupational dust exposure are its significant risk factors. Inhaled arthrospores establish the lung infection.
Histoplasma capsulatum

Histoplasma is acquired from moist, nitrogen-rich soil with bird and bat guano and is known in the eastern and central United States. Southwestern dust, road work and these risk factors point to Coccidioides.
Blastomyces dermatitidis

Blastomyces lives in forest soil, decaying wood and manure in the midwestern and southeastern United States and southern Canada, not in southwestern desert dust. The setting and risk factors fit Coccidioides.
Paracoccidioides brasiliensis
Paracoccidioides lives in cool, humid soils of Central and South America and strikes poorly nourished rural farm workers. A southwestern United States road worker exposed to dust fits Coccidioides.

set2.q: A gardener has the forearm lesions shown, which began as a single nodule where a thorn pierced the hand. Which organism most likely caused them?
opts: Sporothrix schenckii

Correct. A thorn puncture, a nodule at the entry site, then a line of lesions up the forearm is lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis: Sporothrix schenckii forms a nodule where contaminated plant material penetrated the skin and spreads to nearby lymph nodes.
Trichophyton species

Trichophyton is a dermatophyte: tinea corporis forms inflamed, red rings on smooth skin after contact with people, clothing or bedding, and stays in keratinized epidermis. A nodule at a thorn prick that spreads toward the lymph nodes is subcutaneous sporotrichosis.
Malassezia furfur

Malassezia furfur is the yeast of tinea versicolor, a superficial mycosis with mild, chronic scaling and mottling of the skin rather than nodules. A thorn wound followed by a nodule and spreading lesions marks Sporothrix schenckii.
Candida albicans

Cutaneous candidiasis develops in chronically moist skin, such as the armpits, groin and under the breasts, and in burn patients; a thorn does not plant it. A nodule at a puncture site that spreads to nearby lymph nodes is Sporothrix schenckii.

set2.q: A patient receiving amphotericin B develops fever, weakness and an arrhythmia. Why does this drug also harm the patient's own cells?
opts: Fungi and humans are both eukaryotes

Correct. Amphotericin B complexes with cell membrane lipids, and because fungi and humans are both eukaryotes the action is not selective enough to attack only fungi. Fatigue, weakness, fever and arrhythmia are its potentially serious side effects, hence the nickname 'ampho-terrible'.
Its target is a cell wall humans share

Humans have no such cell wall; the thicker fungal cell wall is what human cells lack, which is why potassium hydroxide lyses human cells and spares fungi. The drug acts on membrane lipids, which fungal and human cells, both eukaryotic, have in common.
It comes from a fungus, not a bacterium

Amphotericin B is produced by a soil bacterium, Streptomyces, and its source is not what makes it toxic. The toxicity comes from its non-selective action on the membranes of eukaryotic cells, fungal and human alike.
It destroys the patient's normal flora

Loss of normal flora is not the cause given for its toxicity; fever, weakness and arrhythmia are direct side effects. Amphotericin B attacks membrane lipids in eukaryotic cells, human as well as fungal.

mis.Its target is a cell wall humans share: assumes humans have a cell wall

set2.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire fungi of medical importance
set2.q: Paracoccidioides brasiliensis can infect the lungs or the skin. How does the skin infection arise?
opts: Eating crops from contaminated soil

Ingestion is the route of fungal toxins (mycotoxicoses such as aflatoxin), not of Paracoccidioides. Its two routes are inhalation of spores (lung infection) and inoculation of spores (skin infection).
Inoculation of spores into the skin

Correct. Lung or skin infection with Paracoccidioides occurs through inhalation or inoculation of spores, respectively: inhaled spores infect the lungs, and spores inoculated into the skin infect the skin. Rural farm workers and harvesters are most at risk.
Inhalation of spores from soil dust
Inhalation is the route to the lung infection, not the skin infection. The two routes map one to one: inhalation gives lung disease, and inoculation of spores into the skin gives skin disease.
Spread from an infected family member

Most fungal pathogens need no host to complete their life cycles and are generally not communicable; person-to-person spread is a feature of dermatophytes and Candida. Paracoccidioides skin infection follows inoculation of spores.

set2.q: After a presumptive diagnosis of candidiasis, how are the Candida species told apart?
opts: A potassium hydroxide mount

A potassium hydroxide mount lyses human epithelial cells and leaves the thicker-walled fungal cells intact, showing that fungus is present. It reveals the yeast, but growth on selective, differential media is what differentiates the Candida species.
Selective, differential media

Correct. A presumptive diagnosis rests on budding yeast cells and pseudohyphae, but growth on selective, differential media differentiates the Candida species. The smear shows a Candida infection; culture on these media names the species.
A negative stain for a capsule
A negative stain demonstrates the capsule of an encapsulated budding yeast, the sign of Cryptococcus neoformans. Candida species are told apart by growth on selective, differential media.
Wood's light on infected hairs
Wood's light on hairs is a step in working up hair, skin and nail specimens, the territory of the dermatophytes. Candida species are separated by growth on selective, differential media.

set2.q: A 9-year-old has the scaly patch shown, with hair lost over it. Which name fits this ringworm?
opts: Tinea versicolor

Tinea versicolor, despite its name, is a superficial mycosis caused by the yeast Malassezia furfur, with mild, chronic scaling and mottling of the skin. Scalp ringworm with hair loss in a child is tinea capitis, a dermatophytosis.
Tinea capitis

Correct. Ringworm of the scalp, tinea capitis, affects the scalp and hair-bearing regions of the head; hair may be lost, and it is common in children. The child's age, the scalp location and the hair loss over the lesion all fit.
Tinea barbae
Tinea barbae is ringworm of the chin and beard of adult males, contracted mainly from animals. A scaly scalp patch with hair loss in a child is tinea capitis.
Tinea corporis

Tinea corporis forms inflamed, red ring lesions anywhere on smooth skin and spreads by contact, clothing and bedding. The hair-bearing scalp of a child, with hair loss, is the territory of tinea capitis.

set2.q: In an immunocompromised patient, where does Cryptococcus neoformans spread after the lungs, with the gravest results?
opts: The meninges and brain

Correct. Lung infection by Cryptococcus neoformans brings cough, fever and lung nodules; dissemination to the meninges and the brain can cause severe neurological disturbance and death in compromised hosts.
Nearby lymph nodes

Spread from a skin nodule to nearby lymph nodes is the lymphocutaneous form of sporotrichosis, which starts at a puncture wound. Cryptococcus neoformans moves from the lungs to the meninges and brain.
The sinuses and ear canals
Colonizing the sinuses, ear canals, eyelids and conjunctiva is typical of Aspergillus, alongside fungal balls in the lungs. Cryptococcus neoformans is feared for spreading to the meninges and brain.
The nail beds of hands and feet

Persistent colonization of the nails of the hands and feet, distorting the nail bed, is tinea unguium, a dermatophyte infection. Cryptococcus neoformans disseminates from the lungs to the meninges and brain.

set2.q: Beyond the lungs, which progression is typical of chronic blastomycosis?
opts: Fungal balls in sinuses and ear canals

Fungal balls in the lungs and colonization of the sinuses, ear canals, eyelids and conjunctiva belong to Aspergillus. Chronic blastomycosis means skin nodules and later bone and nervous system complications.
Thick white growth in mouth and throat

A thick, white, adherent growth on the mucous membranes of the mouth and throat is thrush, caused by Candida albicans. Chronic blastomycosis shows cutaneous nodules followed by bone and nervous system involvement.
Skin nodules, later bone and nerve disease

Correct. Blastomycosis can become chronic, with cutaneous nodules (for example on the hand and wrist) followed by complications in bone and the nervous system. The infection starts in the lungs, where inhaled conidia convert to yeasts.
Lymph node spread from a thorn wound

A nodule at a puncture site that spreads to nearby lymph nodes is lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis, from Sporothrix schenckii. Blastomycosis produces chronic skin nodules and then bone and nervous system disease.

set2.q: A kidney transplant recipient has cough, fever, shallow respiration and cyanosis. A tissue section shows the cysts seen here, each containing several bodies. Which organism is most likely?
opts: Blastomyces dermatitidis

Blastomyces dermatitidis is a dimorphic true pathogen whose inhaled conidia become yeasts in the lungs, at times mistaken for lung cancer on chest X-ray. Cysts holding several bodies in a transplant recipient point to Pneumocystis jirovecii.
Pneumocystis jirovecii

Correct. Cysts containing several bodies are the tissue form of Pneumocystis jirovecii, a small, unicellular fungus. Kidney transplant patients are at high risk, and cough, fever, shallow respiration and cyanosis are its pneumonia, in which secretions block breathing.
Cryptococcus neoformans

Cryptococcus neoformans appears as an encapsulated budding yeast on negative stain and causes cough, fever and lung nodules before spreading to the meninges. Cysts each holding several bodies identify Pneumocystis jirovecii.
Aspergillus fumigatus
Aspergillus grows as branched septate hyphae with conidial heads and forms fungal balls in the lungs. Rounded cysts containing several bodies, not hyphae, point to Pneumocystis jirovecii.
